## The decision in one sentence

`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/drop_in.cljc` is a 418-line public, tested, undocumented, unconsumed adapter that lets "a host that is NOT a re-frame2 app" pump trace events into Xray's buffer; either write the spec it never had (A: a §Drop-in trace source in 013, an API.md row, manifest rows) or delete it with its 251-line test (B).

## The problem, carefully

**What the file is.** One namespace, eight public vars: `attach!`, `detach!`, `emit!`, `attached?`, `current-mode`, `normalise-event`, `collect-from-host!`, `reset-for-test!` (drop_in.cljc:125, 165, 210, 217, 299, 313, 378, 408). Its docstring (lines 11-19) promises that "an XState app, a Redux app with a logger middleware, a Zustand app with a devtools subscription, a custom state-machine harness" can plug into Xray and "the panels (Epoch, Trace, App-db diff, Machine, ...) light up against the host's events exactly as they would against a native re-frame2 event-bundle."

**The three modes** (drop_in.cljc:43-69, 226-295):

1. `:push` — `(attach! {:mode :push})` records the mode; the host then calls `(drop-in/emit! event)` per event. `emit!` throws `:rf.error/xray-emit-before-attach` if called while detached (lines 398-404).
2. `:atom` — `(attach! {:mode :atom :trace-source <atom>})` `add-watch`es a host atom holding an append-only vector; on attach it pumps the atom's current contents, thereafter only the new tail of each `swap!` (lines 234-284). CLJS-only; the JVM arm throws `:rf.error/xray-atom-mode-requires-cljs` (line 358).
3. `:sub` — `(attach! {:mode :sub :trace-source (fn [emit-cb] -> unregister-fn)})` hands the host a collector callback and keeps the returned unregister fn for `detach!` (lines 286-295).

All three funnel into `collect-from-host!` (line 165), which fills a missing `:id` from a private counter and a missing `:time` from `interop/now-ms` (lines 118-145), then calls `trace-collector/collect-trace!` — Xray's own trace-listener body (line 189). Every entry is gated on `rf.interop/debug-enabled?`.

**What host it was built for.** Its first commit is `9df55062d1` (2026-05-21, PR #1777, "feat(causa): drop-in mode for non-re-frame2 apps with trace bus (rf2-1o9cq)"). That bead is no longer in the live tracker (identity hits 0 in `.beads/issues.jsonl`; recovered from export commit `07f0700820`): "[causa][v1.1] Drop-in mode for non-re-frame2 apps that expose a trace bus", created 2026-05-13, P4, whole description: *"Stately Studio 2026 visualises Redux/Zustand without XState. Causa could embed any state-machine shape that hits its trace bus — not only `reg-machine`-registered ones. A drop-in Causa for a non-re-frame2 app that just exposes a trace bus. v1.1+ direction."* Source: `ai/findings/sweep-tools-vs-sota-2026-05-13.md §causa` — a competitor-parity sweep; the doc no longer exists locally. Its one note (2026-05-14) **deferred it to 2026-08-05**: "v1.1+ feature — embedding any state-machine shape via the trace bus is a substantial cross-cutting change (touches trace-bus.cljc API, registry semantics, **panel projections that today assume reg-machine shape**). Best landed with the v1.1 design pass; no need to short-circuit." It was closed six days later, close reason in full: "Landed in #1777 admin". So this was a P4 "keep up with Stately Studio" idea, marked v1.1+, deferred because the panels would need to change, then landed a week later with the pump half only — the deferral note names the very gap the code still has (see *Make it tangible*). The 14 commits since (`git log --follow`) are all repo-wide sweeps that happened to touch it — Causa→Xray rename, `:rf.error/id` shape, the rf2-43koh trace-bus retirement, rf2-lvqmw's "make `emit!` strict" posture polish, docstring de-historicising, egress profiles, alias canonicalisation. None added a consumer.

**Consumer census (measured, with control).** Ripgrep for the namespace or any of its public vars (`re-frame2-xray\.drop-in|re_frame2_xray/drop_in|drop-in/(attach!|emit!|detach!|attached\?|current-mode|normalise-event|collect-from-host!|reset-for-test!)`) across the whole tree: **3 files** — `.beads/issues.jsonl`, `drop_in.cljc`, `drop_in_cljs_test.cljc`. Control, the same search for `re-frame2-xray\.preload`: **55 files** (54 in the tree — src, tests, testbeds, specs, docs, skills, workflows, `spec/api-manifest*.edn`). Case-insensitive `drop-in|drop_in` reads 38 files, and every hit outside the two above is the English phrase ("drop-in replacement", "drop-in consumer", `:drop-internal?`), checked line by line for the Xray-, Story- and pair-mcp-adjacent ones (`skills/re-frame2-pair/preload/re_frame2_pair/runtime.cljs:2758`, `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/shadow_discovery.cljs:99`, `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/filters/typed_predicates.cljc:386`, `tools/xray/spec/Principles.md:170` — the last names `drop_in.cljc` only as a carrier of the `debug-enabled?` self-gate). `XState|Zustand` reads 151 files: all machines-DSL parity, migration docs and conformance fixtures; the only Xray-facing text promising a non-re-frame2 *host* is drop_in.cljc's own docstring. `non-re-frame|not a re-frame2 app|hosts that are not` over docs/, skills/, tools/xray/spec: only the migration skill's "Dependencies changed (non-re-frame)" lines.

**Spec census.** `tools/xray/spec/013-Trace-Consumer.md` headings enumerated (23 of them, lines 1-710): no `§Inputs`, no drop-in heading — the docstring's link at drop_in.cljc:23 points at a heading that does not exist. `tools/xray/spec/API.md`: 0 mentions, while its §Wider public surface (API.md:306-315) calls itself "the **complete** index so a reader scanning for 'what's publicly callable?' has a single authoritative list". `tools/xray/README.md`: 0. Manifest: Xray IS in the repo-level manifest — 49 `day8.re-frame2-xray.*` rows over 17 namespaces in `spec/api-manifest.edn`, curated as `:cljs-only` rows in `spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn` — and `drop-in` reads 0 in both. Nothing flags that absence: `tools/xray/src` is not under `roster-covered-roots` (gen.clj:299-308), so the roster-completeness gate never asks about it.

**Two further facts the reviewer did not record:**

- The three `:rf.error/*` ids the file mints (`xray-atom-mode-requires-cljs` :358, `xray-unknown-drop-in-mode` :369, `xray-emit-before-attach` :400) are the **only** `:rf.error/xray-*` ids in the tree (ripgrep: 2 files, both drop-in; `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` 0). Xray otherwise mints no error ids; these three are uncatalogued anywhere.
- A latent ordering defect. The drop-in numbers events from its own `id-counter` starting at 0 (drop_in.cljc:118-121), independent of the framework's private `event-counter` (implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc:53). Xray's snapshot merges the framework rings with the frameless ring and **sorts by `:id`** (trace_collector.cljs:230; 013:272-276). So a host event pushed at minute ten carries id 1 and sorts ahead of every framework event in the buffer. The tests order drop-in events only among themselves (`multiple-emits-preserve-order`, test :112-120). Reading of the code, not executed.

**Who it affects.** No programmer today (zero callers). Under A it becomes a promise to programmers writing non-re-frame2 apps; under B nothing observable changes for anyone in this repo.

## Make it tangible

**What the framework already offers.** Spec 009 §Emitting trace events (spec/009-Instrumentation.md:988-996): "The framework emits trace events through one entry point: `re-frame.trace/emit!`. **User code may also call it (re-exported as `rf/emit-trace-event!`) to add custom events to the stream.** … The runtime stamps `:id` and `:time` … and synchronously invokes every registered listener." The facade exists (core.cljc:2300) and is rowed in the hot-zone `spec/API.md:655` as `(emit-trace-event! op-type operation tags)`, v1 dev-only, tooling tier. Xray's collector is one of those listeners, registered through the public facade — `(rf/register-listener! :trace :rf.xray/trace-collector trace-collector/collect-trace!)` (install.cljs:52-53) — and a frameless emit "SKIP[s] the framework's per-frame rings — they stream to listeners only" (013:243-245), landing in the same frameless secondary ring drop-in feeds.

So push mode, side by side:

```clojure
;; drop_in.cljc today (its own docstring example, lines 330-334)
(drop-in/attach! {:mode :push})
(drop-in/emit! {:operation :xstate/transition :op-type :machine :tags {:from :idle :to :playing}})

;; the documented framework door, no attach ceremony, framework-stamped :id / :time
(rf/emit-trace-event! :machine :xstate/transition {:from :idle :to :playing})
```

Atom mode is `add-watch` plus that one call; subscribe mode is the host calling that one call from its own callback. The ~60 lines of lifecycle at drop_in.cljc:234-295 are what the framework door does not give you, and a host writes them in three.

**What a Redux host actually sees under A, as the code stands.** Xray's `open!` "No-op (returns nil) when no substrate adapter is installed — hosts that never called `rf/init!`" (core.cljs:78-80). So the "host that is NOT a re-frame2 app" must `rf/init!` with a substrate adapter before any panel exists — at which point it is a re-frame2 app with a frame. Then: drop-in feeds only the trace collector (drop_in.cljc:189), never the epoch collector (install.cljs:169), so the **Epoch panel** (epoch records) shows nothing; the **App-db diff panel** reads `(rf/app-db-value frame-id)` (API.md:528) — nothing; the **Machine panel** reads `:rf/machine?` registrations (API.md:531) — nothing. Drop-in events "carry no `:frame`" (drop_in.cljc:174-176), so they reach the frameless ring (capacity 100, 013:261-268) and surface in exactly one place: the `:ungrouped` pseudo-cascade of the L2 event list, and only when `:show-ungrouped?` is on — default `false` (013:255-259; config.cljc:1116). That is the whole delivered capability: a hidden-by-default pseudo-cascade in one list, with the ordering defect above. The docstring's "panels light up exactly as they would against a native re-frame2 event-bundle" is not what the code does, and a §Drop-in trace source written honestly would have to say so.

**What a spec reader sees today.** API.md:516-520 §Trace / epoch surfaces: "Xray **consumes** the framework's surfaces. It does not expose analogues; users go to the framework for these." Drop-in is an ingest analogue Xray exposes. 000-Vision.md:255: "Not a Stately editor / exporter." The one product statement that would justify the file — the Stately-Studio-visualises-Redux idea — lives only in a retired P4 bead and a findings doc that no longer exists.

## Options

### A. Keep it and document it

## Recommendation

**B.** Argued from the stance: minimal API means Xray should not carry a second, undocumented ingest door beside the framework's documented one; "don't litigate the minutiae" says the cheapest defensible option wins, and B is a deletion with one parenthetical edit. The file was a P4 competitor-parity idea marked v1.1+, implemented in a day, and in four months and 14 sweep commits nobody — not Story, not pair-MCP, not a testbed, not a doc — has called it. Its docstring promises a capability the code cannot deliver (Xray will not open without `rf/init!`; only one hidden-by-default list ever shows the events; the ids sort wrongly), it contradicts API.md's own posture that Xray exposes no analogues, and it mints Xray's only error ids without cataloguing them. ## Codex Recommendation

**Recommend B: remove the adapter and its dedicated tests.** The reason is the absence of a demonstrated integration worth maintaining, combined with a mismatch between this ingest path and today's Xray architecture. This recommendation does not authorize deletion during this research task.

**Research basis.** Independently inspected the working tree on 2026-09-17; final revision sampled was `327b74ac6b54d6f6693951da6bf680f157171d5d`. Read `bd show rf2-y8doi.31`, its history, the adapter and tests, the framework emitter, Xray consumers, and relevant git history. The dossier's conclusion is reasonable, but several premises need qualification.

**Verified findings and corrections**

- **No in-repository integration was found.** A namespace/path/public-call search outside `ai/` and `.beads/` found only `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/drop_in.cljc` and `tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/drop_in_cljs_test.cljc`. The API index and manifest pair contain no drop-in entry. That supports low local removal cost; it does not establish that no programmer anywhere uses it. Git history independently confirms introduction in `9df55062d1` and rewiring from the separate trace bus to the current collector in `ca715249f1`.

- **The ingestion limitation is stronger than the dossier describes.** Drop-in preserves supplied tags and passes the normalized map straight to the collector (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/drop_in.cljc:142`, `:186`). It does not enforce the comment's claim that host events lack a frame. The collector retains an event in its secondary ring only when BOTH `[:tags :frame]` and `[:tags :rf.trace/dispatch-id]` are absent (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/trace_collector.cljs:120`). Otherwise it assumes the framework already stored that event (`:337`). Drop-in never performs that framework storage. Consequently, adding a frame or dispatch ID to an otherwise accepted host event can make it disappear from the snapshot. This is a static control-flow finding, not a reproduced runtime failure.

- **Filling the buffer does not provide the promised panels.** The Trace tab itself reads a focused epoch record through `:rf.xray/epoch-history`, rather than the flat trace buffer (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/trace.cljs:1206`). Epoch collection is a separate listener (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/install.cljs:169`), and the machine chooser needs registered machine metadata (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/machine_inspector.cljs:985`). Drop-in supplies none of those structures. Mounting also requires an installed substrate adapter (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/mount.cljs:1044`). That is an integration requirement, not proof that a Redux host must become a re-frame application. Merely tagging events with a frame would not repair the integration.

- **The independent counter is a real design mismatch.** Drop-in starts its own counter at zero (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/drop_in.cljc:118`), while merged snapshots sort all producers by numeric ID (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/trace_collector.cljs:230`). Interleaved host/framework traces therefore lack a shared chronological ordering and can reuse IDs. The ordering test covers only three consecutive drop-in emissions (`tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/drop_in_cljs_test.cljc:112`); it does not validate coexistence with framework events.

- **The framework emitter is the appropriate existing path for live custom events, but is not a lossless substitute.** Spec 009 explicitly supports user emission (`spec/009-Instrumentation.md:988`), and Story actually uses it (`tools/story/src/re_frame/story/play/runner_events.cljc:443`). It constructs fresh IDs/timestamps (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc:710`); drop-in preserves supplied ones. Removing drop-in thus removes lifecycle convenience and direct envelope ingestion. It does not remove the supported live-emission path. Xray's listener must still be installed to collect frameless emissions (`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/install.cljs:52`); neither API alone supplies a general external-app debugger or recorded-trace replay facility.

**Options and tradeoffs**

1. **B, recommended:** remove the source/test pair and the reference in `tools/xray/spec/Principles.md:170`. Add a short discoverability note pointing live custom instrumentation to Spec 009, including the existing Xray-installation and ungrouped-view requirements. This reduces concepts for programmers and AI assistants without inventing a replacement abstraction.
2. **Keep a deliberately limited adapter:** correct the public promise, document its useful visibility, and settle storage/identity semantics. Preserving supplied envelopes versus re-emitting live events is a substantive choice. This is justified only by an identified consumer needing the convenience; documenting the current file alone is insufficient.
3. **Build general external-host inspection later:** begin with one real host and one useful panel. Keep that product decision separate from preserving this namespace. Git retains the implementation if its watch/subscription mechanics become useful.

The pre-alpha posture favors B: one established emission path and tools whose claims match their behavior. Avoid adding a compatibility shim, broader ingest protocol, or exhaustive validation for an integration nobody in this repository currently exercises.

**Validation limits.** Evidence is static source/spec/test inspection, repository searches, and read-only tracker/git queries. No application probes, test suites, browser sessions, or production-elision checks were run. External consumers and future product commitments remain unknown. Competitor claims were not needed for this recommendation and were not used as evidence.

title: Incomplete: failed Story assertions still lack Evidence links despite retained beats
description:
Merged-PR audit of #9795 (8dd880a697184e7461147d9a0807ad420049db92). The closed rf2-7etf3 claim is INCOMPLETE: the UI now preserves and consumes a coordinate, but normal canonical assertion records still omit it, so a real failed assertion has no Evidence link even when its own beat is retained.

Reproduced independently on the landed tree, with the real plain-atom adapter and epoch artefact loaded, history depth 50, no stubbed runner: register an event setting :count to 2 and a variant with {:script {:script [[:dispatch-sync [:audit/set]] [:assert-db [:count] 99]]}}. story/run returns :fail and four retained epochs, including the :rf.assert/path-equals event at dispatch-id 6. Its assertion record has neither :dispatch-id nor :epoch-id; test-mode.pure/assertion-row therefore has neither, and evidence-spine/row->beat-index returns nil. row-evidence-link consequently renders no button. This is not the intended no-retained-evidence fallback.

Root cause: tools/story/src/re_frame/story/assertions.cljc:382 dispatch-id-from-cofx reads :dispatch-id or :rf/play-dispatch-id from the coeffects map. The shared core router assemble-initial-ctx at :910-929 supplies neither; it binds the real dispatch identity in trace/*handler-scope* around handler execution (:3261). The assertion wrapper calls the obsolete cofx lookup (:1175), so the record loses identity before the UI projection sees it. These are shared CLJC paths.

Positive control: only for a second real run, temporarily read the already-bound handler-scope dispatch-id in that private lookup. The record then carries dispatch-id 12, matching its retained assertion epoch, and the unchanged row projection/resolver selects beat 3. Both runs retain four epochs. Diagnostic exited 0 after asserting the broken original and successful control; no repository implementation was edited. Separate existing Story UI/Evidence tests pass 82 tests / 372 assertions, showing why their fabricated-coordinate coverage misses this producer gap.

Correction: stamp the canonical assertion record from the actual current dispatch identity using an existing internal context/scope source; do not invent identity from payload equality or add a public coeffect merely for the UI. Add a real run-to-row-to-Evidence regression, including a non-first retained beat and the existing no-coordinate fallback. Keep the bounded UI change already landed.

Evidence artefact: audit-merged-pr-audit-a-pr9795-real-row-3.clj and matching .log/.exit in the audit scratch directory. No mayor notification or acknowledgement is inferred from filing/pushing this finding.
acceptance_criteria: A real canonical assertion failure with retained epoch evidence carries its actual dispatch coordinate on the run result; the projected failed row resolves to the matching non-first beat and its UI link opens that beat. Exercise shared JVM and CLJS paths with runtime-produced records, not only hand-authored coordinates; coordinate-less or unretained rows still show no fabricated link.

The bounded UI change from PR #9795 stays as landed. DOCS/SPEC: none required unless the 017 Run result section states that assertion records carry no coordinate — if it does, one clause. The expected beat is located by trigger event, never by dispatch id.

- clj-kondo --fail-level error: exit 0, 0 errors and 0 warnings.

CONTROL.
- Plant: the lookup was made to ignore the handler scope. It was verified before running: the anchor count read 0 and the blob hash changed.
- JVM: exit 1, 2 failures, all in the retained-beat test.
- CLJS: the recompile exited 0; the test run exited 1, with 3 failures, all in the retained-beat test.
- The fallback tests stayed green in both runs.
- Restore: the file was restored from HEAD. The restored file's blob hash 3dbb8988aeacd6271b30008d1aebd281dea2947b equals the committed blob, and git diff --quiet exits 0.

SPEC — no clause needed.

title: story: rename unreg-global-decorator! — a fresh un-* prefix Conventions :1306 forbids (rf2-uimu follow-up)
description:
Filed 2026-09-06 by the rf2-uimu ruling (delegated by Mike, ruled by the dossier agent). Worker-scoped application of the Lifecycle-verb law, not a decision: the law already forbids this spelling. Sequence AFTER rf2-uimu's Conventions PR merges, so the amended law text this cites is on main.

## Problem
`re-frame.story/unreg-global-decorator!` (tools/story/src/re_frame/story.cljc:766 at tip 13884f326f) is a fresh `un-*` prefix -- exactly what spec/Conventions.md §Lifecycle-verb law :1306 forbids ("file a bead against this section rather than coining `dispose-` / `teardown-` / `shutdown-` / a fresh `un-*`"). It sits on the Story facade (spec/api-manifest.edn:530, `:facade? true`, tier :tooling, owner 007).

Shape, measured: its twin `reg-global-decorator` (story.cljc:731) is registrar-shaped and has no bang (§Naming bucket 1) -- it registers the decorator body via `rf.story.registrar/reg-decorator*` AND appends `[id & ref-args]` to the global-decorators config vector (`rf.story.config/add-global-decorator!`). `unreg-global-decorator!` removes ONLY the vector entry (`rf.story.config/remove-global-decorator!`), is idempotent, and leaves the body registered -- that is `unregister!` (:981, `[kind id]`) 's job.

## Target
Name it by the ladder (Conventions :1299-1305 at tip; re-anchor by text after rf2-uimu lands), not by taste. Step 1: "drop registrations / a cache → `clear-*`; remove one hook by id → `unregister-*`". Default, per the rf2-uimu dossier: **`clear-global-decorator`** -- `clear-*` is the roster's stated symmetric inverse of `reg-*` and the add half here is `reg-global-decorator`; no bang, because the `reg-*` twin has none and the bang axis is decided per pair, not per direction. Use `unregister-global-decorator!` ONLY if the worker shows the global-decorators vector is a runtime hook table the framework invokes from arbitrary call sites (bucket 2) rather than a registrar-shaped config entry -- and say so in the PR body. Do not coin a third spelling; if the ladder is genuinely ambiguous, note it here and stop.

`re-frame.story/unregister!` (:981) uses a rostered verb; confirm it needs no change and leave it.

## Deletion list
The `unreg-global-decorator!` spelling. Pre-alpha: no alias, no deprecation shim (posture: a redundant spelling is deleted, not deprecated).

## Consumers (measured 2026-09-06 at 13884f326f; re-measure)

## Files to touch
story.cljc; tools/story/spec/API.md (if that spec keeps a Removed / renamed ledger, add one line; do not add a shim); docs/story/api/reference.md; docs/story/api/registration.md; spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn + regenerated spec/api-manifest.edn; any test that calls it; any skill that teaches it.

## Hot-zone
None of the files above is on the hot-zone list. Do NOT touch spec/Conventions.md (rf2-uimu owns it) or spec/API.md.

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.4 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.4 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.4 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.4) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/xray filters, theme, settings, diff, palette and chart that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: [GH #11170] re-frame2-pair: the Walk-this-event recipe omits :rf.cofx/generated (recordable coeffect) traces
description:
GitHub issue #11170 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/issues/11170), opened 2026-10-13 by mike-thompson-day8: "Pair cascade recipe omits generated recordable coeffect traces". Close the issue when the fix merges.

THE DEFECT. skills/re-frame2-pair/references/recipes.md, section "Walk this event — what happened when I dispatched X", says injected coeffects appear as "one :rf.cofx/run op per supplier that ran". The implementation has two supplier paths (implementation/core/src/re_frame/cofx.cljc, around :889, `run-ambient-supplier` and `run-generator`):
- ambient suppliers emit `:rf.cofx/run`, with supplier timing;
- recordable generators emit `:rf.cofx/generated`, without `:rf.cofx/elapsed-ms`;
- a supplied or replayed recorded fact need not invoke its generator at all.
Following only `:rf.cofx/run` misses a generated fact, and can lead an agent to conclude its supplier never ran.

THE FIX. Teach both ops in the recipe, and distinguish a generated fact from a supplied or replayed one. Keep `:rf.event/run-end`'s `:rf.event/coeffects` as the delivered user-coeffect map, and say that a missing supplier trace alone does not establish a missing input. Re-derive the op names and the cofx.cljc sites at tip before writing. Check whether any sibling reference in the same skill (ops.md, vocabulary.md, errors.md) repeats the "one :rf.cofx/run per supplier" claim, and fix those in the same commit.

REGRESSION CHECK. The issue asks for a focused documentation regression check. Add one ONLY as a single pin in the skill's existing prompt-regression suite (skills/re-frame2-pair/tests/), asserting that the recipe names `:rf.cofx/generated`. Do not build a new gate.

Gates: scripts/check_doc_slugs.py, the skill's bb test suites, and the api-manifest skills check.

title: Unit-test pruning: mcp-base
description:
Apply Mike's pruning prompt to tools/mcp-base/test recursively in an isolated worker worktree. This is a distinct cluster in rf2-0wcq5. Push a test-only draft PR, babysit all checks until green, then mark ready; do not merge. Report no-op with evidence instead of manufacturing changes.

Simplify the unit tests under tools/mcp-base/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside tools/mcp-base/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
tools/mcp-base/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in tools/mcp-base/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If tools/mcp-base/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside tools/mcp-base/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Routing guard sub traces and :rf.nav/push-url fx args carry a declared sensitive path param raw
description:
Two routing trace surfaces still carry a declared sensitive path param raw, after PR #11284 (rf2-zpe22) redacted `:requested-url` on the blocked, denied and `{:url}` fallback traces.

Measured by the rf2-zpe22 worker with a scratch scan of every trace emitted for a route declaring `/reset/:token`, across the URL-driven, `{:url}` and `{:to}` navigation doors. The fix was applied, and a guard was set up to block or deny.

1. Guard sub traces. `guard?` appends the resolved target to the guard query, so `:rf.sub/run` and `:rf.sub/dispose` carry `query-v [guard-id target]`, and that target's `:params :token` and `:url` are raw. This happens on every block and every denial, through every door.
2. `:rf.nav/push-url` fx args. On a committed `{:url}` or `{:to}` navigation, and on an ambiguous route's fail-closed `{:url}` navigation, the token appears raw in two places: the `:rf.fx/do-fx` trace's `:rf.event/fx`, and the `:rf.fx/args` of `:rf.fx/skipped-on-platform` (JVM).

Scope: no always-on record carried the secret in any case scanned, so both are dev-time trace surfaces. The blocked and denied event vectors are already redacted by their registration's `:sensitive` declaration.

Decide per surface whether the routing layer should hand traces a redacted projection, or whether the trace is correctly carrying the app's own data. Fix only what the redaction contract in Spec 012 / Spec 009 says must be redacted, and record the reasoning for any surface left alone.

Files likely: `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/` (the `guard?` query construction; navigate.cljc's push-url fx), plus a routing test namespace. Fenced on #11284 merging, because that PR edits navigate.cljc and decisions.cljc.
notes:
== RULING (worker, 2026-10-15 23:36 AUSEST): both surfaces are carrying data the contract leaves open by design. No code change, no spec change, no PR. Recommend closing as working-as-specified.

Verified at source at origin/main d685885a26. None of the cited files changed between the dispatch base 0873ad50a9 and that tip.

SURFACE 1: guard sub traces (:rf.sub/run, :rf.sub/dispose carrying query-v [guard-id target]). LEFT ALONE.
- Spec 012 §The guard sub receives the resolved target as an argument (normative): "The runtime subscribes the guard with the resolved target appended to its query vector — (subscribe [<guard-id> <target>]) ... target is {:route-id :params :query :fragment :url}." decisions.cljc guard? does exactly this: (conj (vec query) target) handed to :subs/subscribe-once.
- Spec 015 §A subscription's query vector is identity, and it egresses raw: "A query vector therefore ships verbatim on every query-vector-bearing slot: :rf.sub/query-v on :rf.sub/run, :rf.sub/skip, and :rf.sub/dispose; ... epoch capture rows, which key on the query vector". It also rejects both remedies: "Do not attempt to close this by routing the query vector through the sub classification chokepoint ... nor does it blanket-scrub :rf.sub/query-v at egress".
- Code agrees: core classification project-sub-tags projects :rf.sub/value and :rf.sub/prev-value only, never :rf.sub/query-v.
- Why routing cannot fix it at its own seam: the query vector IS what the guard receives, and it is the sub-cache key. A redacted query vector would hand the guard a redacted target, which breaks the 012 guard contract. A projection of one trace slot would still leak through the sibling slots 015 lists, including epoch rows.
- The guard's own error traces (:rf.error/can-leave-non-boolean, :rf.error/can-enter-non-boolean, :rf.warning/can-leave-subs-artefact-missing) carry :query WITHOUT the target, so they are clean.
- Closing this would mean changing what the guard receives (the 012 guard contract), or adding an arg-rooted declaration axis, which 015 says the framework deliberately does not provide. That is a design decision, not a redaction fix.

SURFACE 2: :rf.nav/push-url fx args (:rf.fx/do-fx :rf.event/fx, and :rf.fx/args of :rf.fx/skipped-on-platform on the JVM). LEFT ALONE.
- Spec 012 §Route data classification, the paragraph beginning "It covers the navigation events and URL strings that name the route". It names exactly which URL strings the route's declaration reaches: "the URL-change argument, a request's :url, the planned :url". It then says: "Other ambient traces from the same navigation stay wide open by design: ... the fx args on :rf.fx/handled (:rf.nav/push-url's URL string, :rf.nav/scroll's target address) ... because each of those slots is governed by its own registration's :sensitive declaration (015 §Registration-owned transient classification) rather than by the route's."
- Spec 015 §Registration-owned transient classification: "An fx's classification covers every fx-arg-bearing trace slot at egress — not just :rf.fx/handled", naming (2) the :rf.event/fx aggregate on :rf.fx/do-fx and (3) :rf.fx/skipped-on-platform. So the two measured slots are governed by push-url's registration, the same as :rf.fx/handled. Code agrees: core classification project-trace-event walks :rf.event/fx and any [:rf.fx/id :rf.fx/args] slot through project-fx-args, which reads the fx registration's declaration.
- push-url's registration declares nothing on purpose. The nav_fx.cljc push-url-meta docstring says "We deliberately DO NOT mark it :sensitive", because the pushed URL is the navigation's behavioural identity: the :effects-routed conformance contract and the epoch :effects projection assert the actual routed URL.
- The declared-path-param case was considered when the declared-URL redactor was introduced (commit 940f8334f1). That commit kept push-url's URL string in the wide-open list, and its message says "The dispatched event, the committed URL and the route slice stay raw ... every other ambient carrier stays as it was".
- The same reasoning covers the ambiguous-route fail-closed {:url} push. It also covers routing's own non-owner / JVM-client :rf.fx/skipped-on-platform :url tag in nav_fx history-mutation-handler, which carries the same path-form URL on purpose: its comment says "the failure/skip traces keep the path-form url — the navigation's behavioural identity".
- Redacting here would need either a fourth dynamic per-fx-id classification in core (015 names exactly three: :dispatch, :dispatch-later, :rf.http/managed) or a reversal of the 012 sentence above. Both are contract changes outside this bead.

No Spec 012 redaction sentence is wrong, so the spec is untouched. The routing JVM lane baseline at 0873ad50a9 was exit 0, 280 tests / 991 assertions. Nothing was changed, so no gate was re-run.
close_reason:
Working as specified: no change. The dispatched worker checked both surfaces against the contract at origin/main d685885a26 and found each deliberately unredacted.

(1) Guard sub traces (:rf.sub/run and :rf.sub/dispose carrying [guard-id target]).
- Spec 012 §The guard sub receives the resolved target as an argument requires (subscribe [<guard-id> <target>]), with :params and :url.
- Spec 015 §A subscription's query vector is identity says query-v ships verbatim on :rf.sub/run and :rf.sub/dispose. It rejects both routing query-v through the sub classification chokepoint and a blanket egress scrub.
- Core's project-sub-tags projects only :rf.sub/value and :rf.sub/prev-value.
- Redacting at routing's seam would hand the guard a redacted target, and would change the sub-cache key.

(2) :rf.nav/push-url fx args (:rf.event/fx on :rf.fx/do-fx, and :rf.fx/args on :rf.fx/skipped-on-platform).
- Spec 012 §Route data classification lists push-url's URL string among the slots that "stay wide open by design", each "governed by its own registration's :sensitive declaration".
- push-url-meta is deliberately not :sensitive, because the :effects-routed conformance contract asserts the routed URL.

title: Split the conformance runner by posture so its trace-free fixtures run in the production-gate lane
description:
FENCE: do not dispatch until PR #11275 (rf2-u4qcq) AND rf2-puy70's PR both MERGE. Both edit the conformance runner or how it sits in the gate. Clears when both merge.

The conformance runner could be split by posture, returning about 119 fixtures to the production-gate lane. Found by the rf2-u4qcq worker on 2026-10-15. Under `-Dre-frame.debug=false`, 121 of 240 conformance fixtures fail, because the runner reads traces, effects-routed and the SSR public error off the dev trace, epoch records off the trace-fed ring, and the live graph and schema validation, all dev-gated. #11275 therefore tags the whole `re-frame.conformance-test` dev-only. A production claim set that does not claim `:core/trace` or epoch would let the ~119 gate-passing fixtures run in the prod-gate lane, which is real production coverage.

Change: in implementation/core/test/re_frame/conformance_runner.cljc, select fixtures by the capabilities they claim, and run the subset that claims neither trace nor epoch under the gate. Keep the dev-posture run exactly as it is. Count the fixtures that move, and raise RF2_MIN_TESTS by that amount if they count as tests.

Posture check before starting: if the split needs more than a small claim-set filter, stop and report rather than build machinery. P4: worth it only if it stays small.
notes:
== POSTURE-CHECK STOP (2026-10-16 00:38:21 AUSEST) — measured at origin/main 418fae5495, no code changed, no PR

VERDICT: stopped under the item's own posture rule. The fixtures that pass under -Dre-frame.debug=false are NOT separated by a claim-set predicate, so the split is not "a small claim-set filter".

MEASUREMENT. Every corpus fixture graded through re-frame.conformance-runner/run-corpus-fixture with the JVM leaf's host map, in a JVM started with -Dre-frame.debug=false (interop/debug-enabled? read back false): 241 fixtures, 1 skipped (ssr-render-tree-hash.edn, allowlisted), 119 pass, 121 fail. No passer was missed by any predicate below.

1. The claim-set predicate the item proposes — claims neither :core/trace nor epoch — selects 190 fixtures: 119 pass, 71 FAIL. There is no epoch capability in the vocabulary at all (epoch is asserted through the :epoch-records expect key, not claimed). :core/trace splits 0 pass / 50 fail, but 118 fixtures assert :trace-emissions and only 48 of them claim :core/trace: 70 fixtures assert traces without the tag (counter-inc-once.edn, the routing-*, http-managed-*, resources-*, ssr-*, schema-*-validates families among them). The 71st is derivation-graph-algebra-full.edn (below). This is not a tagging defect: the README defines :core/* as pattern-required basics every port supports, so :core/trace says nothing about which fixtures need the dev trace — capabilities model what a PORT supports, not the debug posture.

2. An EXPECTATION-KEY predicate does separate them: a fixture whose :fixture/expect names none of :trace-emissions, :effects-routed, :epoch-records, :ssr/public-error selects 120 fixtures, 119 pass and 1 fails. The one failure is derivation-graph-algebra-full.edn, whose second :derivation-graph call runs :mode :live — dev-gated by design (re-frame.derivation.graph/live-derivation-graph's docstring: the live projections are gated on interop/debug-enabled? and the graph is empty in production). Excluding the :derivation/algebra-graph capability (0 pass / 1 fail; the narrow :derivation/algebra-graph-subs-machines fixture is static-only and passes) makes it 119/119 clean.

3. The 119 are not vacuous: 101 carry :fixture/calls (Mode-B pure-call assertions — machine transitions, routing match, image assembly, CEDN-1 identity), 23 carry a non-empty :fixture/expect (app-db, runtime-db, sub-values, absent paths), none carry neither.

WHAT BUILDING IT WOULD TAKE, if the expectation-key form is wanted instead: a predicate over :fixture/expect keys plus the :derivation/algebra-graph exclusion (a few lines in conformance_runner.cljc); a second, untagged deftest in re-frame.conformance-test running that subset; and a per-posture runnable floor, since run-corpus asserts (>= (count run) 150) and the subset is 119. RF2_MIN_TESTS would move by 1, not by 119 — fixtures are not tests (run-corpus is one deftest emitting three assertions however many fixtures it grades). That is a ruling for Mike: the item ruled a claim-set filter, and this is not one.
== RULING AND BUILD (2026-10-16 01:00:45 AUSEST) — PR #11312

RULING (Mike, through the mayor, after the posture-check stop above): build the EXPECTATION-KEY split in place of the claim-set premise; the stop was correct, the claim-set premise was wrong, and the expectation-key split is small enough for the item's posture.

BUILT. conformance_runner.cljc: prod-posture-fixture? selects a fixture whose :fixture/expect names none of :trace-emissions, :effects-routed, :ssr/public-error, :epoch-records (dev-posture-expect-keys) and which does not claim :derivation/algebra-graph (dev-posture-capabilities; its :mode :live call reads the dev-gated live derivation graph). run-corpus takes the runnable floor as an optional fourth argument; the three-argument form keeps 150, so the dev-posture whole-corpus run (^:requires-debug, JVM and CLJS) is unchanged. conformance_test.clj: a second, UNTAGGED deftest run-conformance-corpus-prod-posture runs the subset with floor 115 (119 selected, minus 4 of slack, about RF2_MIN_TESTS's proportion). scripts/test-core-prod-gate.sh: RF2_MIN_TESTS 1047 -> 1048 for the one deftest added. TESTING.md unchanged: its production-gate row never called the conformance test dev-only.

COUNTS. Core prod gate before 1082 tests / 2654 assertions, after 1083 / 2657 (the predicted +1 / +3; slack 35), both exit 0. Core JVM lane (clojure -M:test) exit 0, 1188 tests / 3674 assertions. clj-kondo on the two changed files exit 0, 0 errors / 0 warnings.

title: Unit-test pruning: skill-retro
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside skills/re-frame2-pair-retro/tests that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Keep routing and resource allocation usable without the optional Schemas artefact
description: Audit of PR #11351 confirms the documented LinearLite pilot cannot run against this merged tree as written. workspace.md explicitly drops the Schemas coordinate for LinearLite, consistent with routing/resources packaging contracts. However nav-allocation-cofx-meta and pending-nav-allocation-cofx-meta in routing/nav_counters.cljc and generation-allocation-cofx-meta in resources/state.cljc still declare Malli :schema values. Core cofx/validate-recordable-value! intentionally throws :rf.error/schemas-artefact-missing when such a declaration has no loaded validator. Consequently the pilot's first navigation refuses before baseline counts, and schemas-free routing/resource consumers encounter the same coupling. The source records reproduce exit 1 without Schemas and green runs after a real dependency/preload was added only to ignored test workspaces; PR #11351's 9/18 green is not evidence that the published schemas-free assembly works. This defect predates the test pruning. Small correction follows the existing rf2-rtqyb ruling: keep declared user cofx schemas fail-closed, remove Malli declarations from these three framework allocation cofx, and structurally validate generated/supplied/replayed allocation shapes on every consuming handler path before any state commits. Preserve malformed-fact refusal and schemas-optional packaging. Source records already propose PR #11354; reuse and verify that repair rather than adding mandatory Schemas or starting a competing redesign. Acceptance: the published LinearLite assembly runs its pruned 9-test/18-assertion baseline with no re-frame.schemas/Malli runtime, and the existing allocation record/replay refusal guards remain effective.

title: Use canonical :error reply payloads in the login-form Story failure seeds
description: Audit of PR #11349 found an existing mismatch in tools/story/testbeds/login_form/stories.cljc:202 and :234. Both the error and submitting-retry variants dispatch [:login/failure {:failure {...}}]. The receiving :record-error action in events.cljc destructures :error, and the shipped HTTP canned-failure producer (implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/test_support.cljc, emit-canned-failure!) emits {:status :error :error (assoc tags :kind kind)}. Thus these advertised simulated server replies never supply their declared message to the action. They appear correct only because their message equals the action's fallback, Invalid credentials.; changing that fixture message has no effect on the rendered error state. Small correction: seed both variants with the canonical :status/:error envelope and classified HTTP failure map. Give the existing error scenario a distinct supplied message and update its retained projection expectation so the same scenario proves that message is actually consumed; preserve all five scenario states, retry attempts and HTTP stubbing. This is a concrete teaching-fixture correction, not a request for broader test coverage or a production API change.

title: Teach the :initial-events start kick for machines read at first paint, and retire the hand-rolled definition-fallback advice
description:
## Ruling

Keep the `nil` contract for a machine that has not been born. `@(rf/subscribe [:rf/machine id])` stays `nil`, and `[:rf.machine/has-tag? id tag]` stays `false`, until the machine's first event or its `[id [:rf.machine/start]]` kick. Where a view needs a live machine at first paint, the one taught answer is the start kick in the frame's `:initial-events`. Machines nobody reads at first paint stay lazy. There is no runtime change and no new diagnostic. The docs, the login Story and the improver skill currently teach three different answers; they will teach this one.

Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned

> review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section.  Where the original recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision.  And then remove the file.  Leave behind cases where the two differ materially.

Decisive facts, at trunk 89517e8f54:

1. **A definition projection is not what birth produces.** Both framework subs read the stored runtime-db snapshot and nothing else (`implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc:296-312`). A runtime sub's fn receives only `(runtime-db query-v)`, with no frame or registrar access (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/subs.cljc:402-419`). The definition seed, `build-initial-snapshot` (`implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/parallel.cljc:383`), runs no `:entry` and no `:always`/`:raise` settle. Birth is `apply-initial-entry-cascade` (`parallel.cljc:1891`). So a projected seed shows a transient or `:choice` initial the machine never rests in, and it lacks any `:entry`-seeded data.
2. **The kick already exists, is one line, and lands before the frame is handed back.** `:initial-events` run synchronously before `make-frame` returns (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc:3481-3489`; pinned by `implementation/core/test/re_frame/frame_initial_events_cljs_test.cljc:60-66`). Spec 005 already names them as the home of a boot-time singleton's kick (`spec/005-StateMachines.md:2779-2781`; `spec/Pattern-Boot.md:224`).
3. **The docs teach three answers today.** `docs/machines/concepts.md:258-259` tells a view to "fall back to the definition's `:initial` and `:data`" by hand. Spec 005 at L142 and Pattern-Boot say kick. The improver skill says kick AND a default branch, "both required" (`skills/re-frame2-improver/references/boolean-discriminator-subs.md:111`). A census of `examples/` and the testbeds finds 0 views that hand-roll the definition fallback.

For orientation: XState's views never see `undefined` because `createActor` computes the settled initial snapshot where the view's context is created (XState v5.20.2, `packages/core/src/createActor.ts`, `packages/core/src/StateMachine.ts`). Nothing projects a definition. re-frame2's creation site is the frame, and its counterpart of `createActor(m).start()` is the kick in `:initial-events`.

Rejected options:
- **B. The subs serve the definition's initial snapshot before birth.** Rejected: the unsettled seed shows transient initials and omits `:entry` data (Xray's Static Machines Sim had to add a disclaimer for exactly this seed, rf2-00126, `tools/xray/spec/003-Machine-Inspector.md:1465`). The settled form would run user `:entry` and guard code inside a subscription. Either way the view disagrees with runtime-db, Xray and the pair MCP, a finished or destroyed singleton reads as freshly initial, and the subs would need frame-aware definition lookup they cannot do. That is a breaking contract change across three hot-zone files, for a benefit confined to machines with no birth work, where `nil` is already harmless.
- **C. A declared eager-birth option such as `:start :eager`.** Rejected: new machinery. Registration would gain a side effect into live frames, against "The handler stays registration-free" (`spec/005-StateMachines.md:4278`). It needs a multi-frame and SSR policy, and it duplicates what `:initial-events` already does. Blanket eagerness is out entirely, because `:rf.http/managed` registers as a machine purely to be spawned (`implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/machine_wrapper.cljc:199`).
- **A new diagnostic for a lazy first-paint start.** Rejected: the `:rf.machine/started` trace's `:cause :lazy` already surfaces it, and Xray renders it as a `[START]` badge. Trust the programmer.

What would reopen it: a real app whose machine-registering module cannot reach any frame-setup event (that argues for an opt-in C, not B); or a recurring consumer that must display an unstarted machine without running its effects (that argues for a separately named pure preview API, like XState's `initialTransition`, not for changing the instance sub).

Supersedes no ruling or EP. It resolves the item that ruling rf2-29hkz explicitly left open ("nil-before-birth … A UX call").

## Work

Teaching surfaces only. No spec, runtime or test change.

1. **`docs/machines/concepts.md:258-265`.** Delete "A view that renders earlier should fall back to the definition's `:initial` and `:data`." Teach instead that a view needing the machine at first paint starts it where the frame is created, with the kick in `:initial-events`, and replace the bare `(rf/dispatch [:auth.login/flow [:rf.machine/start]] {:frame login-frame})` "at startup" example with:

   ```clojure
   (rf/make-frame {:id :app
                   :initial-events [[:auth.login/flow [:rf.machine/start]]]})
   ```

   Keep the sentences after it on what the kick runs (`:entry` fires, `:after` timers arm, it never matches an `:on`, and `:entry` sees `[:rf.machine/start]` as `:event`). Add one clause saying a machine nobody reads at first paint can stay lazy.
2. **`docs/machines/coming-from-xstate.md`.** Row L50 (`actor.getSnapshot()`): say the sub reads `nil` until the machine is born. Row L54 (`createActor(machine).start()`): XState computes the settled initial snapshot at `createActor`, so `getSnapshot()` is never `undefined`; re-frame2's creation site is the frame, so the counterpart is the kick in the frame's `:initial-events` (and the first event still births a machine lazily).
